item.title: Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans
item.description:
Elon Musk has quietly funneled more than $276 million into Republican groups and his super PAC since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.

The staggering amount of money makes Mr. Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Mr. Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Thursday.

In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, he gave a total of $158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team. In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.

Mr. Musk has also built a major Republican turnout operation through a super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. He donated over $76 million this summer to the group, which in turn spent that much on building a sprawling canvassing program to try to turn out hard-to-reach Republican voters. The group is active in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races.

Sources: Federal Election Commission filings (prior contributions), representatives for Mr. Musk (most recent contributions).

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Mr. Musk has already given far more money, about $366 million, to federal committees during the 2025-26 election cycle than he did during the 2024 election, when he laid out roughly $290 million to help return President Trump and Republicans to power. He has given even more in undisclosed donations during both elections, according to people briefed on the giving.

The latest torrent of spending has helped give the Republican Party a financial advantage in the midterms, as well-funded outside groups like Mr. Trump’s powerful super PAC flood the airwaves with advertising in the final weeks. No Democratic billionaire is spending nearly as much as Mr. Musk, and money remains a central worry for the party in an otherwise favorable political environment.

The donations also clear up the mystery of how much staying power Mr. Musk wants to have in American politics.

“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.

Mr. Musk, who oversees a vast business empire that has benefited from enormous federal contracts, is famously unpredictable and often jumps from one project to another. He has been far quieter about his political work since his dramatic blowup with Mr. Trump last year. After months of wielding vast influence inside the White House and overseeing Mr. Trump’s government cost-cutting project, he raged against the president’s major domestic policy bill and floated threats to start a third party.

But the two men have warmed back up, appearing together at three events in the last two weeks and praising each other.

Now Mr. Musk has donated more than a quarter-billion dollars to help Mr. Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The money signals his commitment to the right and sets him up as a potential player in the 2028 presidential election, when his super PAC says it intends to remain active — the first time it has confirmed such plans.

Beyond Mr. Musk’s donations to his super PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund, his representatives said that from July through September, he had given smaller but still substantial amounts to other conservative groups:

$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans

$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas

$10 million to the Republican Governors Association

$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” said Andrew Romeo, a spokesman for America PAC. “These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”

On voters’ doors across Texas, the campaign literature carries a stark warning: “Radical Democrat socialists are winning elections all across America. Could Texas be next?”

The hanging door cards are the work of Mr. Musk’s voter-turnout operation, which deployed nearly 3,000 paid canvassers last week around the country, according to America PAC officials.

The group has devoted most of its more than $76 million in midterm spending so far to this canvassing program, shelling out smaller amounts on advertising, mail, phone calls and text messages. Much of the messaging targets Democrats, sometimes in misleading or overheated ways.

This spring, Mr. Trump’s political advisers asked Mr. Musk to reprise America PAC’s 2024 field program, a person familiar with the conversation said. Despite the challenging environment for Republicans, some party strategists believe that a field program can make the difference in particularly tight races.

America PAC relies on a few voter-canvassing firms that compete aggressively with one another for work and for staffing, according to people briefed on the operation.

Turnover in the canvassing industry is high. One canvasser who worked for America PAC told The Times that he was paid between $1.50 and $3.00 for each door he knocked on across Texas in the heat. America PAC says it has knocked on about 6.5 million doors across the country so far.

Mr. Musk and his operation, people close to them say, have been particularly focused on the Texas Senate race. The group has unloaded over a third of its disclosed spending in that expensive race, more than in any other. It is uncommon to run an extensive field campaign in large states like Texas, where television ads are more often used to reach voters.

Mr. Musk, a resident of Austin, has extensive business interests and property holdings in Texas. Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, has investigated Mr. Musk’s opponents, like Media Matters, a liberal group.

Mr. Musk’s $10 million donation to Mr. Paxton’s super PAC came at a critical time, when the Republican candidate was being badly outspent.

And Mr. Musk’s $158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Mr. Paxton after months of reluctance.

That is because Mr. Musk’s donations preceded the decision in late August by the super PAC, led by allies of Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, to start what has become a $149 million pro-Paxton ad campaign.

As it did in 2024, Mr. Musk’s operation is focused not on persuading swing voters, but on registering and turning out voters with conservative beliefs — especially “low-propensity” ones who are less likely to cast a ballot.

This is a lot harder for Republicans in a midterm election, without Mr. Trump at the top of the ballot.

To do it, Mr. Musk’s super PAC is leaning hard into the culture wars, especially transgender issues. (Mr. Musk’s daughter, who is transgender, has spoken about their clashes over her identity, and he has suggested that this led to his increased political engagement.)

At voters’ doors in Texas, canvassers are told to target Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, over her record on transgender issues, according to parts of a script reviewed by The Times.

Similarly, the Musk operation is leaving literature on doors that claims that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, has a “radical trans agenda.” And America PAC’s top ad in the state, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, denounces Mr. Talarico over his past comments suggesting that “God is nonbinary.”

The Musk group is also targeting other Democratic Senate candidates over transgender issues, including Josh Turek, the party’s nominee in Iowa. Nationally, one of the super PAC’s most visible ads on Facebook features a man in makeup and reads: “He made his plan to vote. Did you? Don’t stay home while crazies elect radicals.” The group is running ads and sending mail on a broad range of topics, but socialism is a core theme. The Musk super PAC regularly attacks Democrats as socialist and ties them to figures like Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, according to 48 pieces of direct mail shared by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm.

Online, it is even running personalized messaging that invokes a voter’s first name. For example, in a video showing smiling Democrats: “Why are they smiling? Because Christopher hasn’t made a plan to vote yet.”

Much of this outreach points voters to an America PAC website where conservatives can learn about how to register to vote. The super PAC is pushing what it calls an “America Pass,” a digital card on Apple or Google wallets on voters’ phones that lists their registration information, along with election dates and deadlines in their home state.

While Mr. Musk is spending big again and using some tactics that are similar to those he deployed two years ago, this is not 2024 anymore.

He is in a different place politically. While he and Mr. Trump appear to be on good terms again — “our modern-day Thomas Edison,” the president called him on Thursday — Mr. Musk is taking a hands-off approach this election and does not appear as personally passionate.

He has not brought up the midterm elections or the Trump presidency much in private conversations with friends, according to people who have spoken to him in recent months. He is focused on his businesses, these people say, and he and his business lieutenants have taken a less active role in America PAC’s operations, entrusting major decisions to Chris Young, his top adviser.

And on X, a semi-reliable indicator of where the billionaire’s mind is, Mr. Musk has written just seven direct posts this year about candidates in competitive midterm races, according to a Times review, a far cry from his relentless calls throughout 2024 to elect Mr. Trump. Five of those posts focused on Mr. Talarico — and one appeared critical of Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican in Maine.

Gone, too, are Mr. Musk’s barnstorming campaign stops, like the ones he did in Pennsylvania in October 2024 or a Wisconsin judicial election in the spring of 2025. There are no more sweepstakes where he personally hands an oversize check of $1 million to those who register voters or sign a petition, a gambit that drew legal challenges.

Mr. Musk has not evidently grown infatuated with candidates this time around, as he did with Mr. Trump. The closest he came was a $10 million donation for a long-shot Republican running for the U.S. Senate in Kentucky — an investment that went poorly.

The $276 million figure is, of course, just what is publicly known. Mr. Musk has also made some seven-figure donations to support midterm candidates through groups that are not required to disclose their donors, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

Juliana Castro Varón contributed analysis.

item.title: One Grieving Mother, Two Mariners Tickets and a Season of New Friends
item.description:
On the last Sunday afternoon of September, Rhenda Strub was bundled up against the autumn chill for one final day at the ballpark, eating Cracker Jack and sweet and spicy pickles.

Another baseball season was ending as it often does in Seattle: abruptly and too soon. There would be no postseason for the Mariners, the only franchise never to have appeared in a World Series.

A. Bartlett Giamatti, a literary scholar who served as commissioner of Major League Baseball for five months until he died suddenly in 1989, famously wrote that baseball is “designed to break your heart,” because it “leaves you to face the fall all alone.”

Yet this season, Ms. Strub, 71, found that the opposite was also true: Baseball can help heal a broken heart.

After she lost her 27-year-old son, Wyatt, to muscular dystrophy three years ago, she retreated to his room and spent countless hours alone quilting and watching baseball games on television. The constancy of baseball helped to structure her days, but the loneliness only added to her grief.

So at the beginning of this season, Ms. Strub bought two season tickets to the Mariners in Section 120, on the first base side, thinking she would regularly go with her loved ones to T-Mobile Park. But her husband doesn’t like crowds, and the rest of her family has busy lives.

So she wrote a post on Facebook — with some trepidation, she said, because the “internet can be a cruel place” — asking strangers if they wanted to attend games with her.

“This season ticket adventure is part of me finding my way back out — getting out of the house, being around people, and doing something that brings a little joy again,” she wrote. “Baseball helps me heal.”

The post went viral in April, inspiring stories in local newspapers and on the radio.

Her family worried about her meeting up with strangers. Random people also messaged her with their concerns, offering safety tips.

But her inbox was also flooded with messages from people describing their own stories of loss. A child who died. The passing of mothers, fathers and partners. Failed marriages.

And a shared love of baseball.

“I had so many people contact me with remarkably similar stories,” she said. “They have had some sort of life event that left them feeling unbalanced to deeply grieving. And they didn’t really have someone to go to the game with but loved going to the game.”

“Baseball has a calming effect on them,” she added, “and they want someone to share it with.”

Ms. Strub is a lifelong baseball fan, having grown up just outside Kansas City, first rooting for the Athletics before they moved to California, and then for the Royals when M.L.B. expansion brought the franchise to her hometown. She loved George Brett, the Royals’ star third baseman, and Lou Piniella, who played five seasons for the team.

She and her husband began raising their four children in South Dakota, but moved to Olympia, Wash., 24 years ago in search of better jobs. She had a career as an engineering consultant and retired in 2016. She then began to devote much of her time to taking care of Wyatt, whose health problems worsened steadily until he died in 2023.

By the end of this baseball season, Ms. Strub had attended games with about 30 strangers and found that the people she connected with needed her as much as she needed them. She built an online community, bringing together the people she had met in a private Facebook group, calling the project “Strangers to Friends.”

If she couldn’t attend a game — she had to miss a few when her husband, Mike, had brain surgery — she handed off her tickets to strangers who had reached out to her but didn’t know each other.

She said she was “gobsmacked” by the reaction to her post.

“I have made so many friends this summer,” she said. “I have friends that will be my friends for the rest of my life.”

Over the summer, Jack Barrie, a young documentary filmmaker from Los Angeles, reached out to her. Mr. Barrie, who grew up in Seattle and roots for the Mariners, said he felt Ms. Strub’s story of grieving in public “needs to be shared.” The two began meeting and filming a short documentary, “You Sit Here,” a reference to the words on a silhouette next to her in her original Facebook post.

Already, people are booking games with her for next season.

“I just needed something to snap me out of the fog of grief I was in,” Ms. Strub said. “I don’t ever expect to be over his death. I don’t expect to ever recover. But I have been able to find joy again.”

Others found joy through her.

One woman who has a disabled child came from Australia to meet Ms. Strub at the ballpark. Steve Hayburn, a probation officer from Ketchikan, Alaska, flew to Seattle in September after the death of his father and the dissolution of a long relationship.

“When I saw her story, I knew I had to connect with her,” Mr. Hayburn, 55, said. “She kind of reminded me of my mom.”

They met up at the stadium for the second to last game of the season, on a Saturday night. Ms. Strub walked in with her cane, her hat on sideways, a pink chain around her neck holding her cellphone. “She kind of reminded me of a gangster, the way she was walking,” he said.

They watched the Mariners play the Los Angeles Angels and shared a tub of popcorn. “It was like I was spending time with my mom all over again,” he said.

Mr. Hayburn, who grew up in Ohio and rooted for the Cincinnati Reds, added, “It helped me deal with my trauma I’ve been through this year.”

Another new friend, Sheila Cook, lost her wife, Michelle, a few years ago, also to muscular dystrophy. Ms. Cook was shattered by the loss and felt angry and confused about why doctors told her Michelle was ineligible for a heart transplant.

Then she met Ms. Strub, who explained the disease in a way that finally made sense to her. (Ms. Strub also has three grandsons who have been diagnosed with the disease, having passed it down through her daughters with a mutation on one of her X chromosomes, she said.)

“We were just weeping and crying all the way to the ballpark,” said Ms. Cook, 74, who has a dog named after Ken Griffey Jr. “It was a wonderful gift. I truly believe it was a gift from God, that Rhenda was a gift from God.”

In the middle of the summer, the Mariners honored Ms. Strub as their season ticket holder of the year. For one night, she moved up from her regular seat to watch the game with friends in a luxury suite.

She was also asked to throw out the first pitch at that game. It was a nerve-racking proposition because she had never learned to throw properly.

It turned out that one of her new friends, Liz Brown, was a retired schoolteacher who had once taught gym class. So before Ms. Strub took the field at T-Mobile Park, Ms. Brown met her near her home in Olympia and taught her how to throw a baseball.

At the ballpark on the final day of the season, Ms. Strub stood to cheer for one of her favorite players, the pitcher Logan Gilbert, who was being removed from the game in the fifth inning.

Then she continued talking about her son, Wyatt, who had enjoyed going to a ballgame with family even though baseball wasn’t really his thing. He loved online games and singing and acting, and as a teenager, he had appeared in several musicals, including “South Pacific,” “The Sound of Music,” and “Peter Pan.”

“He always played the strong voice character,” she said.

All day at the game, the Mariners played tributes on the video board for Rick Rizzs, the longtime radio voice of the team who was retiring after 41 seasons. Fans offered testimonials about how they, like Ms. Strub, turned to baseball in their grieving. Ms. Strub noted the “constant theme of healing” in the videos and “the peace they found with Rick through baseball.”

Ms. Strub thought more about Wyatt as the game continued.

He had refused to meet with the chaplain as he was dying in the hospital. Then, on his very last day, with hours left, he asked for him.

Wyatt was quiet for a time when the chaplain appeared at his bedside, according to Ms. Strub. Then he turned to the man and said, “You’re not here for me. You’re here for my mom. I need to know she’ll be OK.”

Ms. Strub nodded to her surroundings at the ballpark — the thousands of people around her, the expansive green lawn, the ballplayers.

“This is me trying to be OK for Wyatt,” she said. “I know he’s with me. I can feel him all the time. This is a peaceful place where I can connect with him and feel joy.”

Rhenda’s social media post asking if strangers wanted to attend Mariners games with her went viral at the start of the season, but rather than write about it then I had the idea to wait until September and attend the very last game of the season with her. I found she built a community of people who found solace in baseball during tough times, and that the people she met needed her as much as she needed them.

item.title: Homeland Security Agents Search Home of Rep. Ilhan Omar
item.description:
Federal agents executed a search warrant at the home of Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Monday, according to three people briefed on the matter, the kind of investigative step the Justice Department has long shied away from so close to an election.

The court-approved search of her Washington-area home comes after Department of Homeland Security officials said in recent months that they were investigating Ms. Omar, a Democrat, over her family’s immigration paperwork. More recently, some federal investigators have also sought to investigate other issues, such as Ms. Omar’s finances, campaign funds and interactions with a foreign citizen, as The New York Times previously reported.

The three people who described the execution of the search warrant spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss it.

The search warrant, executed 22 days before Election Day, lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge, according to a person familiar with the document.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that Homeland Security Investigations agents — a part of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — executed a judicially authorized search of a home in the Washington area, as part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The spokeswoman declined to comment further.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Jackie Rogers, Ms. Omar’s spokeswoman, did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent by email and text message Monday morning.

In September, Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, said his department was investigating issues surrounding Ms. Omar and her family’s immigration to the United States, and suggested the end result could be deportation.

Ms. Omar was born in Mogadishu, Somalia, in the early 1980s. Her family fled their hometown when she was around 8, as a civil war engulfed the country, according to a memoir she wrote. In the mid-1990s, after spending time at a refugee camp in Kenya, Ms. Omar and her relatives were admitted as refugees in the United States. They started a new life in Minnesota, which is home to the largest Somali diaspora in the United States.

Ms. Omar has long said that suggestions that she and her family committed immigration fraud were false and politically motivated.

“I will say it again so it’s as clear as possible: I’m not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams,” she wrote in a fund-raising email in September.

Monday’s search of her home, which was reported earlier by Fox News, takes place within the 60-day window before an election. Justice Department policy has long urged prosecutors not to take any overt, unnecessary investigative steps that could affect an election during that period — especially if such actions could be taken after the election without causing any harm to the investigation. The guiding principle of the 60-day rule is that prosecutors should exercise caution in regard to politically sensitive cases.

The rule is not absolute, and there are exceptions, such as instances where prosecutors believe evidence could be destroyed, ongoing crimes are being committed, or people are in danger. The rule is also largely an interpretation of Justice Department regulations, and as such has been the subject of significant debate about its exact parameters. For many years, however, Justice Department officials have concluded that a publicly observable search — such as of a politician’s home or business — is the kind of overt activity that should be avoided during the 60-day period.

In the last federal election, Mr. Trump cited the 60-day rule in his own criminal cases to accuse the department of acting improperly in 2024 as he campaigned for election. He and his lawyers, some of whom now run the Justice Department, argued that the special counsel, Jack Smith, broke the 60-day rule when he filed court papers in September 2024 describing the evidence supporting charges that Mr. Trump conspired to obstruct the results of the 2020 election. In that instance, however, the key decisions were made by the courts, which are not subject to the department policy.

Ms. Omar has represented a solidly blue district that includes Minneapolis since 2019, and she faced no serious competitors during the primary this year.

item.title: A Trump Loyalist, a Turkish Investor and a Battle for Wealth and Influence
item.description:
When President Trump’s former personal lawyer, Alina Habba, married a Turkish businessman last month, the lavish ceremony cemented their status as a MAGA power couple.

Ms. Habba, 42, a longtime Trump loyalist, and Turhan Mildon, a 29-year-old investor, hosted some of Washington’s most powerful people, including Attorney General Todd Blanche, the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel.

It was a striking official entry into Trumpworld for Mr. Mildon, who nearly a year ago faced the loss of his extensive business interests in Venezuela because of his ties to the inner circle of Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan leader who was captured by U.S. commandos in January.

It also put a new focus on the intermingling of personal relationships and foreign policy in the Trump era, in this case highlighting a battle for wealth and influence involving well-connected people in both Caracas and Washington seeking to use access to Mr. Trump to their benefit.

Before the United States captured Mr. Maduro, aides to Mr. Trump and some U.S. intelligence officials expressed concern about Mr. Mildon’s work with the Maduro government, according to multiple people briefed on the matter. Mr. Mildon had spent months trying to build ties between Alex Saab, one of Mr. Maduro’s closest confidants in Venezuela, and Republicans in Mr. Trump’s orbit. The Trump administration had considered placing sanctions on Mr. Mildon, two people involved in the discussions at the time said.

Once Mr. Maduro was out of the picture, things for Mr. Mildon got even worse.

Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, ordered an audit of the state-owned cement plants that Mr. Mildon was operating. In June, she issued an order revoking his contract altogether, citing a failure to meet investment targets, according to a copy of the document seen by The New York Times.

At that point, his patrons could no longer protect him. Mr. Maduro was not only out of power, but sitting in an American jail. Mr. Saab, Mr. Mildon’s most powerful ally in Venezuela, was arrested and extradited to the United States.

But there was a bright spot: Mr. Mildon had met Ms. Habba, one of Mr. Trump’s most prominent legal defenders. They started dating this year, soon after Mr. Maduro’s downfall. By this past summer, the couple’s burgeoning romance had begun to draw attention. Specifically, it caught the eye of Ms. Rodríguez, according to two people close to her. Mr. Mildon was in a serious relationship with a woman who had high-level access to Mr. Trump — the one person keeping Ms. Rodríguez in power.

Since taking office, Ms. Rodríguez has been trying to balance the interests of the competing MAGA factions, and gauging their relative influence over Mr. Trump. After learning of Mr. Mildon’s powerful allies, she decided to pause her order terminating his cement contracts, allowing him to continue to profit from them, according to people familiar with her thinking.

A spokesman for Mr. Mildon said the government had never carried out the audit and that his company was only notified of the contract’s termination on Oct. 8, the day The Times began inquiring about the status of his operation in Venezuela.

The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said his client believed the letter was a mistake and that he was working to address the issue. The spokesman also took issue with the suggestion that the United States had considered sanctioning Mr. Mildon, calling it a “totally false and malicious rumor.”

An administration official also disputed whether the government had considered sanctions against Mr. Mildon.

The Venezuelan government did not respond to a request for comment.

White House officials say that Ms. Habba, who now goes by Mrs. Mildon, has not discussed her husband’s business dealings with Mr. Trump or any other White House officials.

“I have never, under any circumstances got involved with this White House or administration on behalf of my husband, nor would he ever ask me to,” she said in a statement.

The U.S. sanctions proceedings against Mr. Mildon were shelved after the regime change in Caracas, overtaken by bigger targets inside the government, according to a person familiar with the matter.

In the meantime, Mr. Mildon’s relationship with Ms. Habba grew closer. In September, they were married, in a ballroom in New York’s Waldorf Astoria hotel.

This article is based on interviews with more than two dozen people with knowledge of the events, most of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the details of the relationship and Mr. Mildon’s business interests.

Mr. Mildon explained his business strategy in an interview published earlier this month with Forbes Turkey. “In my grandfather’s time, know-how, (knowledge) was very important,” Mr. Mildon told the magazine. “Now, know-who (who you know) is important.”

Mr. Mildon grew up in a provincial Turkish town near the strait of the Dardanelles, where his family ran a network of local businesses, including auto-repair shops and gas stations.

His big break coincided with his first marriage, in 2021, to a daughter of a construction magnate close to Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Shortly after the wedding, Mr. Mildon met the president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Félix Tshisekedi, at an event in Istanbul and jumped on an airplane to explore investment opportunities in the country, Mr. Mildon’s spokesman said. He quickly built close ties with the Congolese political elites and won contracts for prominent construction projects.

Mr. Mildon became an adviser to Mr. Tshisekedi in 2023 and obtained a Congolese diplomatic passport. People who have met him in Washington and Caracas said he had on multiple occasions introduced himself as a Congolese official.

Mr. Mildon’s spokesman denied that his client had ever introduced himself as a Congolese official. Congo’s foreign ministry declined to comment.

In late 2023, Mr. Mildon, who portrays himself as a billionaire, flew into the Venezuelan capital at the invitation of a Venezuelan friend.

As he had in Congo, Mr. Mildon quickly made powerful friends. He won the support of the local Turkish ambassador and met the daughter of a powerful admiral.

His most critical relationship was with Mr. Saab, the Maduro confidant who had recently returned to Caracas from an American jail and been appointed as industry minister.

The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said his client had had only professional, and occasional, interactions with Mr. Saab, who was the official responsible for dealing with foreign investors. Numerous people close to the Venezuelan government, however, said the two became personally close.

In March 2025, Mr. Saab gave Mr. Mildon a contract to operate the cement plants.

A few months later, the Venezuelan government awarded Mr. Mildon a shrimp production and export business in western Venezuela. The government had seized the business months earlier from its private founder, José Enrique Rincón, after accusing him of financing the political opposition. Mr. Rincón remains in jail.

The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said Mr. Saab had played no role in the shrimp business award and that Mr. Mildon had participated in a bidding process with four others to obtain the cement business. The spokesman said he did not know who the other bidders were.

Mr. Mildon’s account is disputed by numerous prominent Venezuelan businessmen and people close to the government, who said that Mr. Saab and other Venezuelan ministers handed out state-run assets to private investors without competitive bidding.

As his fortunes rose, Mr. Mildon’s first marriage crumbled.

In June 2025, he became engaged to María Eugenia Ceballos, a Venezuelan admiral’s daughter, Mr. Mildon’s spokesman said. Her father, Adm. Remigio Ceballos, served for years as the operational head of Venezuelan military and is under U.S. sanctions for participating in corruption and human rights abuses.

The Trump administration at the time was escalating economic and military pressure on Mr. Maduro, and Mr. Mildon became increasingly involved in back-channel diplomacy between Washington and Caracas. His efforts put him in a group of multinational businessmen who had sought preferential treatment by ferrying messages between the capitals last year. These intermediaries have included a Brazilian beef billionaire, an American asphalt tycoon and a Venezuelan oil magnate.

Mr. Mildon also began attending social events organized by Republican insiders.

He became a frequent guest at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, where he networked with the man in charge of the institution at the time, Richard Grenell. Mr. Grenell was also working as Mr. Trump’s special envoy to Venezuela, and trying to broker Mr. Maduro’s exit from power.

Mr. Grenell introduced Mr. Mildon to some of the MAGA crowd. Mr. Mildon’s spokesman said his client and Ms. Habba had first met at an event at the Kennedy Center in late 2025, and started dating in early 2026.

Ms. Habba’s ties to Mr. Trump go back years. She met Mr. Trump through his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., and joined his legal team after his first term, representing him in two civil trials. She joined the White House at the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, then served briefly as New Jersey’s interim U.S. attorney.

She has maintained a close relationship with the president to this day, and met with him in the Oval Office last week.

Even as he was meeting Ms. Habba, Mr. Mildon was navigating the shifting political landscape in Venezuela after Ms. Rodríguez had been put in power by the Americans. His spokesman said Mr. Mildon had always supported Ms. Rodríguez, who served as Mr. Maduro’s vice president until his arrest.

But several people who met Mr. Mildon in Washington last year, before Mr. Maduro’s capture by U.S. forces, said Mr. Mildon had praised Mr. Saab, her ruling party rival, presenting him as Venezuela’s pre-eminent power broker and the key to a peaceful resolution of the conflict with the United States.

As it turns out, Mr. Mildon had backed the wrong side.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio sidelined Mr. Grenell and persuaded Mr. Trump to adopt a more aggressive stance toward Mr. Maduro. Mr. Rubio settled on Ms. Rodríguez as Mr. Maduro’s successor, and set in motion plans for a military operation that would topple the Venezuelan president and install her in power.

Mr. Maduro dismissed the growing threats from the White House as a bluff, right until U.S. military aircraft attacked Caracas in the early hours of Jan. 3.

The arrest of Mr. Maduro, and then Mr. Saab, threatened Mr. Mildon’s businesses in Venezuela. The new government accused him of failing to raise output and lower prices. Contractors complained of unpaid invoices.

Mr. Mildon tried to build ties to Ms. Rodríguez. When Christopher Ruddy, the chief executive of Newsmax, a pro-Trump news channel, secured a meeting with her in February, Mr. Mildon tagged along. The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said he has spoken with Ms. Rodríguez several times since.

Mr. Mildon told Forbes Turkey that he produces 4.5 million tons of cement a year in Venezuela. Data seen by The Times shows that Venezuela’s entire annual cement output is about a third of that figure.

He visited one of the cement plants in June, promising to bring new investment and raise output. He wore a red shirt of the type that was ubiquitous among ruling party apparatchiks, but had largely been abandoned since Mr. Maduro was captured. He gave two thumbs-up, Trump style.

Mr. Mildon also claimed in the Forbes Turkey interview that his shrimp business employed 20,000 people and would reach revenues of $500 million in two years. Data seen by The Times, however, shows that in the first eight months of the year the plants sold on average just 5 percent of the shrimp, in terms of volume, that they had been shipping before the government takeover.

After The Times presented Mr. Mildon with the data, his spokesman said Mr. Mildon had been misquoted in the Forbes Turkey article.

As Venezuela evolved, so did Mr. Mildon’s fortunes.

Mr. Maduro was gone. Mr. Mildon’s powerful political backers were fired or sidelined.

His relationship with Ms. Ceballos, the daughter of Mr. Maduro’s longtime military official, also ended. (Adm. Ceballos did not respond to a request for comment. Ms. Ceballos could not be reached.)

But Mr. Mildon’s marriage ceremony to Ms. Habba, which the wedding planners boasted had come together in under 60 days, was a high-profile social event, attracting dignitaries, oligarchs and senior politicians from around the world, who were in New York for the annual meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. Nelly, the Grammy Award-winning rapper, performed.

And Mr. Mildon’s cement businesses are still operating, his spokesman says.

He is working to stave off Ms. Rodríguez’s revocation of his contract. It is a development that he apparently did not expect.

“When no one else had the guts to come, one man did and invested millions,” he said in the Forbes Turkey interview, referring to himself and his business in Venezuela. “They’re not the sort of people who would turn their backs, now that things are better, on a man who trusted them and came here in good faith.”

Reporting was contributed by Justin Makangara from Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Julian E. Barnes and Glenn Thrush from Washington and Benjamin Weiser from New York. Sheelagh McNeill and Safak Timur contributed research.

item.title: Judge Orders Trump Administration to Answer for Tree Removals at D.C. Golf Course
item.description:
A federal judge on Monday excoriated the Trump administration for ripping up hundreds of mature trees at a Washington golf course over the holiday weekend, even though she had directed officials to disclose any major changes before work was started.

In an explosive, four-hour emergency hearing, Judge Ana C. Reyes of the Federal District Court in Washington ordered a one-day halt to any more tree removal at East Potomac Golf Links, and said she would continue proceedings on Tuesday.

But first she directed Justice Department lawyers to track down a succession of progressively more senior officials involved in the decision, and ordered them to testify on the spot, as she demanded answers about who had authorized the trees to be cleared and whether the decision was linked to the White House. President Trump has eyed the municipal course in southeastern Washington for redevelopment into a luxury championship course similar to those on his personal properties.

“I am thoroughly unamused right now,” Judge Reyes said, appearing remotely from Istanbul, where she had been traveling. She raised her voice at several points to near shouting level.

“What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case,” she said, before listing all of the times she had directed the government to alert her to major alterations.

The Monday morning hearing was technically to address the tree removal, but Judge Reyes made clear that her larger concern was the possibility that the Trump administration had flouted her instructions. Since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, judges have repeatedly been forced to interrogate whether the government has complied with orders across a variety of cases.

Two Washington residents and a preservationist organization had sued in February over the president’s stated goal to redevelop the affordable municipal course into a championship-level one. In June, Mr. Trump was photographed touring the grounds and studying blueprints with Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Tom Fazio, a well-known architect who has designed other courses owned by the Trump Organization.

At a hearing in July, Judge Reyes, a Biden appointee, ordered the Trump administration to notify the court before making sudden alterations to the course. She said that she was worried about how quickly plans were taking shape, and that she did not want to find out work had begun too late to “stop the trains.”

On Friday evening, the Justice Department filed documents showing the administration intended to remove 529 trees as part of a larger restoration. By Saturday morning, machinery could be seen cutting down trees. The government acknowledged on Monday that more than 400 were removed in one fell swoop over the weekend.

In a filing on Sunday night, lawyers representing the D.C. Preservation League asked Judge Reyes to block further action, noting that the government had indicated that there were still “hundreds more” trees to be cut, prompting her to call for the emergency hearing.

She fumed at the hearing that she had given the Trump administration “the benefit of the doubt” at every turn to disclose its plans for the course, only to learn while traveling that the government had moved ahead.

When Marissa Piropato, a Justice Department lawyer, could not explain why the government had waited until Friday night to alert the court to action planned for the following day, Judge Reyes reacted furiously.

“Ignorance is not an excuse here,” she said.

She told Ms. Piropato at another point that “what I find most frustrating about this, counsel, is that this is all double speak.”

Judge Reyes said she needed to figure out the chain of events that led to the tree removal, to figure out “whether or not I’ve been lied to.”

One official, Kevin Griess, a National Park Service official overseeing public lands in Washington, testified that plans for the tree removal were finalized on Oct. 5, and that he received the go-ahead to proceed over the weekend from Frank Lands, a deputy director at the National Park Service.

At that point, Judge Reyes ordered that Mr. Lands be located to testify. Appearing remotely from his car in a parking lot, Mr. Lands explained that he formalized plans to renovate the course with Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee at the Interior Department. Mr. Lands said that he and Mr. Wischer had also discussed Mr. Trump’s ideas to remake the site into a premier competition course.

Judge Reyes then ordered Mr. Wischer, a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, to appear, but Ms. Piropato said the department was unable to reach him. At that point, Judge Reyes concluded the hearing for the day, ordering that Mr. Wischer be prepared to testify as early as Tuesday morning.

“We’re going to get him in here tomorrow,” she said.

In the meantime, Judge Reyes blocked the government from removing more trees until 2:00 p.m. on Tuesday, and she said she would consider whether to block to the government from doing any work at the course for two weeks. She added that she would “try and take this step by step.”

She ordered Mr. Griess, Mr. Lands and their staff members to preserve records about the decision, and warned of repercussions if the government did more work at the course on Monday, given her orders to stop.

“I promise you, if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings,” she said.

Judge Reyes said she felt betrayed by the Justice Department after she had repeatedly declined to formally block the Trump administration from conducting work at the site, despite repeated requests from the group that had sued.

“I wanted you all to be better than you have been,” she told Ms. Piropato.

item.title: Actress Selma Blair Is Arrested in Assault on Flight Attendants
item.description:
The actress Selma Blair was arrested late on Sunday after the police responded to a call about a “physically abusive passenger” aboard a flight that had landed at Kennedy Airport in New York, the Port Authority Police Department said.

The police said two flight attendants reported injuries on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York.

One flight attendant was taken to a hospital for further evaluation. Details about the attendants’ injuries were not immediately available.

Ms. Blair, 54, was taken into custody just after 11 p.m. and was then taken to a hospital, the Port Authority Police Department said.

The F.B.I., which is responsible for investigating assaults on airplanes, said on Monday that it was investigating but declined to comment further.

It was not immediately clear what, if any, charges Ms. Blair faces.

Ms. Blair “experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct,” a representative for the actress said in a statement. “Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

The representative did not elaborate about the specifics of what led up to the episode or describe the nature of the medical emergency.

There were no operational issues on the flight. The plane landed ahead of schedule at J.F.K., according to FlightAware, a flight-tracking site.

Delta said in a statement that the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.”

Ms. Blair was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018, an autoimmune disease that attacks the central nervous system.

The actress, who has starred in the movies “Cruel Intentions” and “Hellboy,” has talked openly about the chronic illness, which was the subject of a documentary “Introducing, Selma Blair,” in 2021.

In 2016, Ms. Blair was removed from a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles after a disruptive outburst.

Ms. Blair said in a statement to Vanity Fair at the time that a combination of alcohol and medication caused her to “black out” and “say and do things that I deeply regret.”

item.title: An Ad Targeting Susan Collins’s Opponent Airs in the Wrong Portland
item.description:
A Republican super PAC trying to influence a crucial Senate race in Maine spent thousands of dollars running an attack ad in the wrong Portland, targeting voters thousands of miles away in Oregon.

An ad funded by the super PAC, Defending Main Street, assailing Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine, was shown to more than a million viewers in Oregon and over 300,000 others in Washington State from Thursday to Sunday, according to Google’s advertising data.

The super PAC’s chief financial officer, Sarah Chamberlain, pinned the blunder, which cost $25,900, entirely on its ad-buying vendor, Cross Screen Media. She added that the vendor had pulled the ads, which ran on YouTube, and began a new campaign targeting Mr. Jackson in Maine.

“Defending Main Street had nothing to do with this,” Ms. Chamberlain said in an interview before mentioning 1903 Group, the vendor’s parent company. “They screwed up.”

A spokesman for 1903 Group confirmed the mistake. He said the money had been refunded to the super PAC, which said in a statement that no donor funds would be lost because of the error.

The ad, titled “So Many Taxes,” says that Mr. Jackson supports raising taxes — a line of attack that Senator Susan Collins, a Republican seeking a sixth term, has repeatedly used in her re-election campaign. Ms. Collins is not named in the ad.

“It’s tough to make a living when you pay so much in taxes,” a narrator says in the video. “And taxin’ Troy Jackson made it that way.”

Mr. Jackson has countered that he supports tax increases only on wealthy individuals and large corporations.

People took to social media on Monday morning to share how bizarre it was to have seen the ad in Oregon. Later in the day, the Google listing for the ad appeared to have been fixed, to show ZIP codes in Maine.

Ms. Collins’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Dan Gottlieb, a spokesman for Mr. Jackson’s campaign, seized on the ad mix-up, saying Ms. Collins and “her allies are so out of touch with Maine, they apparently can’t find it on a map.”

Some campaigns intentionally target national audiences to build broader momentum. Ads supporting James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, were shown nationwide in the same period, Google’s ad data showed. But the Maine ad was a pure mistake.

The money spent on the anti-Jackson ads in the Portland, Ore., market paled to the $946,500 that the super PAC recently paid for television and streaming ads opposing Mr. Jackson, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

item.title: Republicans Promoted a False Rumor That James Talarico Was in Ohio
item.description:
After James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, spent more than a week with no campaign appearances because of what he and his aides described as a bad case of the flu, a false rumor circulated by conservatives exploded online.

By Sunday, a post on X claiming that Mr. Talarico had been at a mental health facility in Ohio — a story promoted by Republican allies of Mr. Talarico’s opponent, Ken Paxton — had been viewed millions of times. Then the Ohio facility took the remarkable step of publicly announcing on Sunday night that Mr. Talarico had in fact never been treated there.

“I’ve never even been to Ohio,” Mr. Talarico, who returned to the campaign trail on Friday, wrote in a post sharing the center’s statement. He called the theory “the craziest thing I’ve ever heard” in an interview with MS NOW.

The New York Times reviewed time-stamped images from a security camera at Mr. Talarico’s home, which were provided by his campaign on the condition they not be published for security reasons. The images showed Mr. Talarico at the home between Oct. 1 and Oct. 8.

The episode represented a wild stretch in the Texas Senate race — one of this year’s highest-profile, ugliest and most expensive contests and one that could help decide control of the upper chamber.

The furor over Mr. Talarico’s absence was extraordinary on several levels. It showed how mistrust of politicians and the mainstream news media, combined with online algorithms that incentivize outrageous theories, has created a Wild West of misinformation. It offered a lesson for Democrats: In such an era, it is politically risky for a candidate, even one too ill to campaign, to disappear for nine days.

And it showed how worried Texas Republicans are about Mr. Paxton’s prospects as Mr. Talarico continues to poll ahead of him, despite hundreds of millions of dollars in G.O.P. advertising. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas in more than three decades.

For the first few days, Mr. Talarico’s absence went largely unremarked upon. He appeared in person at a New York fund-raiser on Sept. 29 and the next day, looking ill, spoke virtually at an event, telling attendees that he had come down with the flu.

On Oct. 3, Mr. Talarico’s campaign posted a video of a February rally without clarifying that it was months old, which provoked speculation. (Mr. Talarico’s campaign noted that it regularly reposts social media videos.)

Mr. Paxton increasingly began to fan the flames. Last Tuesday, he promoted a report about Mr. Talarico’s cancellation of a campaign event. On Wednesday, he led supporters in a chant of “Where Is James Talarico?” at a rally with President Trump. And on Friday morning, Mr. Paxton announced a “tip line” for information about Mr. Talarico’s whereabouts.

Throughout it all, Mr. Talarico’s campaign insisted to reporters that he simply had the flu and dismissed rumors that something else might have happened. On Friday, Mr. Talarico reappeared, spending hours at a music festival in Austin, and then went to other public events on Saturday.

In a short interview with The Times, Mr. Talarico said that he had been sick with “a nasty case of the flu” and had been “home sick in bed.”

But that didn’t stop Mr. Paxton’s Republican allies, including Elon Musk and the Trump adviser Stephen Miller, from joining MAGA influencers in flooding social media with posts that questioned Mr. Talarico’s account.

By Sunday, the conservative internet was consumed by an unsubstantiated claim from a right-wing influencer that Mr. Talarico had flown to a mental health facility in Ohio, more than 1,000 miles away from Austin, for treatment of an undisclosed illness. One X post from a Republican consultant and fund-raiser, which pointed to public flight-tracker records about a private jet trip between Texas and Ohio, was viewed 1.8 million times — though the consultant provided no evidence linking the plane to Mr. Talarico.

And two posts from Sunday afternoon of an unverified audio recording, which claimed to provide evidence that a person named James Talarico had been discharged from the facility, were viewed more than eight million times. The claims fell apart hours later, but not before being amplified by Mr. Miller, Mr. Musk, the far-right activist Laura Loomer and a political adviser to Mr. Paxton. Several Republican state lawmakers in Texas also made posts sharing the audio or alluding to it.

“The Talarico campaign is not being honest about what’s happening,” wrote Mr. Musk, who has spent heavily to help Mr. Paxton.

JT Ennis, a spokesman for Mr. Talarico’s campaign, posted online that the claim was “a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory.”

Asked on Fox News whether he would accept a debate challenge extended by Mr. Talarico, Mr. Paxton shifted to talking about his rival’s absence.

“Two weeks is long time to be away with the flu, and it’s just a very strange time to disappear,” Mr. Paxton said on “The Big Weekend Show” on Sunday.

In the interview on Sunday with MS NOW, Mr. Talarico shot back that he had not heard from Mr. Paxton in 85 days about the debate he proposed.

“He has asked for proof of life for me,” Mr. Talarico said. “I’m asking for proof of spine from him.”

On Sunday night, when the Ohio mental health facility posted its statement saying Mr. Talarico had never been treated there, the news interrupted an unusual livestream on X. On the stream, a political adviser to Mr. Paxton, several journalists and others were publicly discussing the veracity of the audio recording, which was posted by Rhein Amacher, who describes himself on social media as a “right-wing provocateur.” At that point, more than 500 listeners were tuned in.

Tony Ortiz, a Paxton supporter and publisher of a right-leaning news outlet, confronted Mr. Amacher, calling his post “sloppy” and criticizing him for releasing the audio. Mr. Amacher had acknowledged on the livestream that he had offered the audio to two right-leaning news outlets but had been refused. Mr. Amacher did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mark Davis, a conservative talk radio host in Texas who has supported Mr. Paxton, wrote on X that the episode should be a lesson for “countless otherwise smart people who publicly accepted the story without question, like baby birds yearning for a worm.”

“Don’t let the fire of battle dull your normal instincts,” Mr. Davis wrote.

An intense, sometimes conspiratorial focus on candidates’ health is “the new normal” in American politics, according to Samuel Woolley, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh who studies how technology manipulates opinion on the web. This has been fueled, he noted, by real concerns about the health of political figures like Mr. Trump, former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky and Representative Thomas H. Kean Jr. of New Jersey.

“It seems that those spreading these rumors don’t care whether or not it’s real,” Dr. Woolley said. “The goal is just to get the story out there and to get people to talk about it.”

Indeed, some Republicans remain undeterred.

“Thanks for breaking the story,” Grant Cardone, a conservative commentator and financial influencer, told Mr. Amacher on the livestream. “Whether it’s true or not, people deserve to see the potential of this.”

J. David Goodman and Steven Lee Myers contributed reporting.

item.title: Calls Show How Confusion Delayed Emergency Response for Christa Pike
item.description:
The emergency response to Christa Pike’s botched execution last month was delayed by about half an hour, because of confusion over the authenticity of the 911 call, according to dispatch and radio calls released on Monday.

The first 911 call for an ambulance was made by someone inside Riverbend Maximum Security Institution at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, about an hour after the lethal injections there began, according to a redacted transcript of the phone call. But confirming the legitimacy of that call took several minutes of back and forth between Nashville emergency services and officials at the prison, according to audio from eight other calls and radio traffic, which was released as part of a public records request by several news organizations, including The New York Times.

The confusion seemed widespread. The initial 911 call did not come, as it might normally, from the central control at the Tennessee Department of Correction, and the caller did not have the right security verification.

In response, dispatch workers repeatedly tried to verify the call by reaching out to prison staff and other officials at the prison during the execution.

“We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening and we need to send an ambulance,” one caller said. Or, she added, “if this is someone that is just basically prank-calling.”

It appears from the phone calls that the Department of Correction’s central control was not immediately aware of the request for help.

One person at central control, who is not identified, tells Nashville emergency services that the department “would have been the one to call you guys — we didn’t call anyone.”

In another call, at 9:03 p.m., someone tells responders that supervisors have said “it is a false call” and that “there is no medical assistance needed.”

But at 9:07 p.m., an emergency responder says as part of radio traffic that “some sort of state official” is “outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in.”

Minutes later, they get word that prison officials have formally confirmed by phone that the request is legitimate.

The Tennessee Department of Correction did not immediately respond to a request for a comment about the apparent breakdown in communication. Previously, the agency said that every step of the protocol had been followed and the process did “not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out.”

Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol has come under renewed scrutiny after the failed attempt to carry out the execution of Ms. Pike, 50, who had been on death row for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate in Knoxville. Lawyers for Ms. Pike, the first person to survive receiving two doses of the drug pentobarbital during an execution, said on Saturday that she had been discharged from a Nashville hospital and returned to prison.

The confusion captured on the calls appear to emphasize how the execution protocol, criticized by state defense lawyers and lawmakers in both parties for its vagueness, does not appear to account for problems during an execution. Tennessee has had two botched executions this year, including Ms. Pike’s.

The protocol really did not consider that the execution may not succeed, said Dr. Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist and intensive care physician who consulted for Ms. Pike’s defense team before the failed execution.

Prison officials, he added, “had no idea that it could fail.”

Dr. Zivot was among the medical experts who warned that Ms. Pike’s underlying medical conditions, including small veins, could complicate the execution. Those warnings were ignored, her lawyers said.

“Considering, of course, what everyone said to them — that it could fail — they certainly did not seem to react,” Dr. Zivot said.

It was not clear from the recordings whether oxygen and other resuscitative gear were on hand in the execution chamber, or if Ms. Pike received medical care before an ambulance arrived more than an hour after the drugs were injected.

The transcript of the initial 911 call and some of the audio recordings were redacted, in part because Tennessee law prohibits the identification of anyone connected with execution procedures. But the person who made the initial 911 call appears unfamiliar with the steps needed to verify the legitimacy of an emergency call from the prison, leading to the effort to authenticate the call.

“Is nobody there that knows the process?” someone asks on a call between the Nashville Fire Department and emergency services.

“I have no idea,” someone else responds. “I guess because this is a special case, they may not know.”

The calls also show that Kelly Gleason, one of Ms. Pike’s lawyers, called 911 at 9:08 p.m., after a colleague who had witnessed the botched injections told her that Ms. Pike was still breathing.

“She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate lifesaving care,” Ms. Gleason said on her call for help. The ambulance drove through the gates a few minutes later.

item.title: 1 Rider Dies and Several Others Are Injured on a Georgia Roller Coaster
item.description:
One rider died and several others were injured on Monday on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, the police said.

The Cobb County Police Department said in a statement that the episode happened at 3:58 p.m. at the amusement park in Austell, Ga., about 17 miles west of Atlanta.

Details about how the rider died, as well as the number of people injured and their conditions, were not immediately available.

A Six Flags representative said in a statement that park officials and the local authorities had responded immediately, but declined to describe what happened, citing the family’s privacy.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the representative said. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends and loved ones.”

The representative also declined to say which roller coaster was involved.

Christina Morales contributed reporting.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Trump, Playing Defense in Ohio, Tries to Shore Up Republicans in Tough Races
item.description:
President Trump returned to Ohio on Monday for the second time in 10 days to play defense in a state that twice helped deliver him to the White House.

He rallied in Youngstown, the heart of the industrial belt that helped fuel his rise, to marshal support for two of the Republican Party’s most vulnerable candidates this cycle: Senator Jon Husted, who is vying to retain his seat, and Vivek Ramaswamy, who is competing for the governorship.

They will need this area to break their way on Election Day in three weeks, with polls showing tight races in a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024 by 11 percentage points.

“Ohio is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it,” Mr. Trump said. “America belongs to those who love it.”

The Mahoning Valley, where he spoke, was battered by globalization. Many voters here grew up as Democrats but became Republicans after Mr. Trump persuaded them that he would fight for them when no one else had. Now, with prices persistently high and Mr. Trump’s approval rating hovering near a record low, officials with both parties see those voters as up for grabs.

“The Youngstown area for decades used to vote Democrat, and then you ran for office in 2016 and flipped it red forever,” Mr. Husted said on Monday in the arena, standing beside Mr. Trump. “Is that right, folks?”

The crowd whooped and cheered. There were at least two sections with large areas of empty seats.

On Monday, Mr. Trump announced two offerings to show voters in the region that he had their back: a new Defense Department facility, which he said would be based in Cleveland, to repair submarine components as well as a promise to make sure that a heat provider for Youngstown remained open.

In other battleground races, including in Michigan and Iowa, Republican candidates have tried to distance themselves from Mr. Trump. But in Ohio, the down-ballot candidates have stayed close to the president, relying on him to turn out the base in a year when Democratic enthusiasm appears to be high.

In addition to Mr. Husted and Mr. Ramaswamy, Representative Max Miller, the embattled congressional candidate accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and young daughter, was in the audience on Monday. (Mr. Miller has denied the allegations.) So was his estranged father-in-law, Senator Bernie Moreno, the Republican who beat Mr. Husted’s Democratic opponent, former Senator Sherrod Brown, two years ago.

Mr. Trump returned the favor by lavishing praise on the candidates — most of all on Mr. Husted, a former football player, who appeared to have impressed the president with his physicality.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said. “I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete.”

item.title: Trump Says He Is ‘Looking at’ Firing Kimberly Guilfoyle
item.description:
President Trump said on Monday that he was “looking at” firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, following revelations that she had asked a Republican donor to pay her credit card bill in exchange for access to senior Trump administration officials.

“Well, we’re looking at it, yeah,” Mr. Trump said when asked by a reporter whether he was thinking of firing Ms. Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.”

The donor, Eric Deters, said last week that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. She promised to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he did, according to what appeared to be screenshots of their correspondence that Mr. Deters provided to The New York Times.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in what appeared to be a text message.

Ms. Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Mr. Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., was one of the first ambassadors to be nominated in the president’s second term.

The texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle warned Mr. Deters to call her on Signal and to keep their interactions private. “You’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship,” she wrote, according to one of the screenshots.

Neither the State Department nor the U.S. Embassy in Athens responded immediately to requests for comment late Monday. A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle previously declined to comment on the correspondence.

The accusations against Ms. Guilfoyle are the latest allegations of misconduct to emerge against her. Greeks interviewed on Athens in recent days have expressed exasperation and cynicism over reports of her dealings.
